bmt-2012-power-1a.title: Forced moves
bmt-2012-power-1a.body:
The vertex $v$ has only one neighbour $u$, so $uv$ is in the matching. Then $m_1$ must be matched to $a_2$ or $a_4$.

- If $m_1a_2$: the remaining vertices $a_1,a_3,a_4$ of the left cluster have no neighbours outside the cluster other than $a_2$ (already used) and $m_1$ (used), so they would have to be matched among themselves, impossible with $3$ vertices.
- So $m_1a_4$. Now $a_1,a_2,a_3$ remain; $a_2$ can go to $a_1$, $a_3$ or $b_1$, but an odd number of the others cannot pair among themselves, so $a_2b_1$ and $a_1a_3$.

By the mirror symmetry, $m_2$ must match $b_3$ (since $b_1$ is used), and then $b_2b_4$.

The matching $\{uv,\ m_1a_4,\ a_2b_1,\ a_1a_3,\ m_2b_3,\ b_2b_4\}$ covers all $12$ vertices exactly once, and it is the only one.

bmt-2012-power-1b.title: Match vertex $1$ first
bmt-2012-power-1b.body:
Let $P(K_{2n})$ be the number of perfect matchings. Vertex $1$ can be matched with any of the other $2n-1$ vertices, and what remains is a complete graph $K_{2n-2}$, so $P(K_{2n})=(2n-1)P(K_{2n-2})$ with $P(K_2)=1$. Hence
$$P(K_{2n})=(2n-1)(2n-3)\cdots3\cdot1=\frac{(2n)!}{2^n\,n!}.$$
For $n=6$: $11\cdot9\cdot7\cdot5\cdot3\cdot1=10395$.

**Answer: $(2n-1)!!$; for $n=6$ it is $10395$**

bmt-2012-power-1c.title: Parity of the outer paths
bmt-2012-power-1c.body:
For $1\le k\le n$ the polygon $\mathfrak P_k$ consists of the edge $v_kv_{k+1}$ and a path $v_k - x_1 - x_2-\cdots-x_{n-2}-v_{k+1}$ with $n-2$ new vertices $x_i$. These $n-2$ vertices can only be matched along the path, or to $v_k$ (via $x_1$) or to $v_{k+1}$ (via $x_{n-2}$).

**$n$ odd.** $n-2$ is odd, so an odd number of the $x_i$ are matched to $\{v_k,v_{k+1}\}$: exactly one of them is. Then the rest of the path is matched in a unique way (consecutive pairs). So each $\mathfrak P_k$ uses exactly one of $v_k,v_{k+1}$; these $n$ polygons need $n$ distinct vertices among $v_1,\dots,v_n$, so each $v_i$ is used by exactly one polygon and no edge of $\mathfrak P_0$ is used. If $\mathfrak P_k$ uses $v_{k+1}$, then $\mathfrak P_{k+1}$ cannot use $v_{k+1}$, so it uses $v_{k+2}$, and so on around. Hence either all $\mathfrak P_k$ use $v_k$, or all use $v_{k+1}$: **$2$ perfect matchings.**

**$n$ even.** Now an even number of the $x_i$ are matched to $\{v_k,v_{k+1}\}$: either none (then the path is matched internally in one way) or both $v_k,v_{k+1}$ are used by $\mathfrak P_k$ (one way for the middle). Let $J$ be the set of edges $v_kv_{k+1}$ whose polygon uses both ends; $J$ is a set of disjoint edges of the cycle $\mathfrak P_0$. The vertices not covered by $J$ must be perfectly matched by edges of the cycle $\mathfrak P_0$, so $J$ together with that matching $N'$ forms a perfect matching $N=J\cup N'$ of the even cycle $C_n$. Conversely, each perfect matching $N$ of $C_n$ and each subset $J\subseteq N$ gives exactly one perfect matching of $Q_n$.

The even cycle $C_n$ has exactly $2$ perfect matchings, each with $n/2$ edges, so the number is $2\cdot2^{n/2}=2^{n/2+1}$.

(A computer count for $n=3,\dots,8$ gives $2,8,2,16,2,32$.)

**Answer: $2$ for odd $n$, $2^{n/2+1}$ for even $n$**

bmt-2012-power-1d.title: Independent set larger than half the vertices
bmt-2012-power-1d.body:
The graph has $10$ vertices. Call the top-centre vertex $T$, the bottom-centre vertex $B$, and the two vertices of degree $5$ in the middle row, second from the left and second from the right, $L'$ and $R'$. Colour $T,B,L',R'$ white ($4$ vertices) and the other $6$ vertices black. Checking the edges one by one, every edge contains at least one white vertex; equivalently no two black vertices are adjacent.

A perfect matching of $10$ vertices has $5$ disjoint edges, and each of them contains at least one white vertex, so we would need $5$ different white vertices. There are only $4$. Hence no perfect matching exists.

**Answer: No**

bmt-2012-power-2a.title: Recurrence
bmt-2012-power-2a.body:
Let $L_m$ be the number of perfect matchings of the ladder with $m$ rungs (so $m-1$ boxes and $2m$ vertices); $L_0=1$, $L_1=1$. Look at the top-left vertex $t_1$ (top-right $t_2$, below them $b_1,b_2$). Either $t_1t_2$ is an edge of the matching, leaving a ladder with $m-1$ rungs, or $t_1b_1$ is, which forces $t_2b_2$ and leaves a ladder with $m-2$ rungs. So $L_m=L_{m-1}+L_{m-2}$, i.e. $L_m=F_{m+1}$.

With $n$ boxes there are $n+1$ rungs, so the number of perfect matchings is $L_{n+1}=F_{n+2}$.

**Answer: $F_{n+2}$** (e.g. $2,3,5,8,\dots$ for $n=1,2,3,4,\dots$)

bmt-2012-power-2b.title: Look at the corner box
bmt-2012-power-2b.body:
Call the corner box's vertices $a$ (outer corner), $b$ (to the right of $a$), $c$ (above $a$) and $d$ (the inner corner, diagonal from $a$). Above the corner box is a ladder $U$ with $n-1$ rungs (attached through $c$ and $d$), and to the right is a ladder $R$ with $n-1$ rungs (attached through $b$ and $d$).

$U$ has an even number of vertices, so the number of its vertices matched downward to $\{c,d\}$ is $0$ or $2$ (both lowest vertices of $U$, matched to $c$ and $d$). Likewise for $R$ and $\{b,d\}$. Both cannot happen, since $d$ would be used twice. So there are three cases.

1. Neither: the corner box is matched internally ($2$ ways: $ab,cd$ or $ac,bd$), and $U$, $R$ are matched independently: $2F_n\cdot F_n$.
2. $U$ is matched down to $c,d$: then $ab$ is forced; $U$ minus its bottom rung has $n-2$ rungs: $F_{n-1}$ ways, and $R$ has $F_n$ ways: $F_{n-1}F_n$.
3. $R$ is matched to $b,d$: symmetric, $F_nF_{n-1}$.

Total: $2F_n^2+2F_{n-1}F_n=2F_n(F_n+F_{n-1})=2F_nF_{n+1}$. (Computer counts for $n=1,\dots,6$: $2,4,12,30,80,208$.)

**Answer: $2F_nF_{n+1}$**

bmt-2012-power-3.title: Symmetric difference of two matchings
bmt-2012-power-3.body: Suppose $M_1\ne M_2$ are perfect matchings of a forest $F$ and consider the set $D=M_1\triangle M_2$ of edges lying in exactly one of them; $D\ne\emptyset$. Every vertex $v$ lies in exactly one edge of $M_1$ and one edge of $M_2$. If these are the same edge, $v$ has degree $0$ in $D$; otherwise $v$ has degree exactly $2$ in $D$ (one edge from each matching). So in the graph $D$ every vertex has degree $0$ or $2$, and since $D$ has an edge, following edges from it never ends and must eventually close up: $D$ contains a cycle. This contradicts $F$ being a forest. Hence $M_1=M_2$. ∎

bmt-2012-power-4.title: Hamiltonian cycle, then alternate edges
bmt-2012-power-4.body:
For $n=1$ the graph is a single edge. Let $n\ge2$.

**Claim: $G$ has a Hamiltonian cycle** (a cycle through all $2n$ vertices). Suppose not, and among all graphs on the same vertex set that contain $G$ and have no Hamiltonian cycle, choose one, $H$, with the maximum number of edges. All degrees of $H$ are still at least $n$, and $H$ is not complete (the complete graph on $2n\ge4$ vertices is Hamiltonian). Pick non-adjacent vertices $x,y$. By maximality, $H+xy$ has a Hamiltonian cycle, which must use $xy$; removing it gives a Hamiltonian path $v_1v_2\cdots v_{2n}$ of $H$ with $v_1=x$, $v_{2n}=y$ non-adjacent.

Let $S=\{i\in\{2,\dots,2n-1\}: v_1v_i\in E(H)\}$ and $T=\{i\in\{3,\dots,2n\}: v_{i-1}v_{2n}\in E(H)\}$. Then $|S|=\deg v_1\ge n$ and $|T|=\deg v_{2n}\ge n$ (since $v_1v_{2n}\notin E$, all neighbours of $v_1$ and of $v_{2n}$ lie among $v_2,\dots,v_{2n-1}$). Both sets are subsets of $\{2,\dots,2n\}$, which has $2n-1<|S|+|T|$ elements, so some $i\in S\cap T$. Then
$$v_1v_2\cdots v_{i-1}\,v_{2n}v_{2n-1}\cdots v_i\,v_1$$
is a Hamiltonian cycle of $H$, a contradiction. So $G$ has a Hamiltonian cycle $C$.

Since $C$ has $2n$ vertices, taking every other edge of $C$ covers each vertex exactly once: a perfect matching. ∎

bmt-2012-power-5.title: Hall's theorem
bmt-2012-power-5.body:
($\Rightarrow$) Let $M$ be a perfect matching and $S\subseteq V_1$. The partners in $M$ of the vertices of $S$ are $|S|$ distinct vertices, all in $\operatorname{adj}(S)$. So $|\operatorname{adj}(S)|\ge|S|$.

($\Leftarrow$) Induction on $k=|V_1|=|V_2|$; $k=1$ is clear (Hall's condition with $S=V_1$ gives an edge). Assume the condition holds for all subsets $S\subseteq V_1$ and the theorem is true for smaller sizes.

*Case 1: for every nonempty proper subset $S\subsetneq V_1$, $|\operatorname{adj}(S)|\ge|S|+1$.* Pick any vertex $x\in V_1$ and any neighbour $y$ of $x$ (it exists as $|\operatorname{adj}(\{x\})|\ge1$), match $x$ with $y$ and delete both. For a nonempty $S\subseteq V_1\setminus\{x\}$, $S$ is a proper subset of $V_1$, so $|\operatorname{adj}(S)|\ge|S|+1$ in $G$, and after deleting $y$ at least $|S|$ neighbours remain. So the smaller graph satisfies Hall's condition and has a perfect matching by induction; together with $xy$ this is a perfect matching of $G$.

*Case 2: some nonempty proper subset $S_0\subsetneq V_1$ has $|\operatorname{adj}(S_0)|=|S_0|$.* Split $G$ into $G_1$, induced on $S_0\cup\operatorname{adj}(S_0)$, and $G_2$, induced on the rest, $(V_1\setminus S_0)\cup(V_2\setminus\operatorname{adj}(S_0))$. In $G_1$, for $S\subseteq S_0$ the neighbours of $S$ lie in $\operatorname{adj}(S_0)$, so $|\operatorname{adj}(S)|\ge|S|$ holds; by induction $G_1$ has a perfect matching. In $G_2$, take $S\subseteq V_1\setminus S_0$. Then $|\operatorname{adj}(S\cup S_0)|\ge|S|+|S_0|$ and $\operatorname{adj}(S\cup S_0)=\operatorname{adj}(S_0)\cup\big(\operatorname{adj}(S)\setminus\operatorname{adj}(S_0)\big)$, so $|\operatorname{adj}(S)\setminus\operatorname{adj}(S_0)|\ge|S|$, i.e. Hall's condition holds in $G_2$, which has a perfect matching by induction. Combining the two matchings gives a perfect matching of $G$. ∎

bmt-2012-power-6a.title: An invariant
bmt-2012-power-6a.body:
We show by induction that $x_n^2+x_{n-1}^2-3x_nx_{n-1}=-1$ and that all $x_n$ are integers. Start: $x_1=x_0=1$ gives $1+1-3=-1$.

Suppose $x_0,\dots,x_n$ are integers and $x_n^2+x_{n-1}^2-3x_nx_{n-1}=-1$ (with $n\ge1$). The recurrence gives $x_{n+1}x_{n-1}=x_n^2+1=3x_nx_{n-1}-x_{n-1}^2$ (using the invariant), so $x_{n+1}=3x_n-x_{n-1}$ (note $x_{n-1}\ne0$ since $x_{n-1}>0$ by induction), an integer. Moreover
$$x_{n+1}^2+x_n^2-3x_{n+1}x_n=x_n^2+x_{n+1}(x_{n+1}-3x_n)=x_n^2-x_{n+1}x_{n-1}=x_n^2-(x_n^2+1)=-1,$$
so the invariant continues to hold. Hence every $x_n$ is an integer (indeed $x_n=3x_{n-1}-x_{n-2}$, giving $1,1,2,5,13,34,\dots$). ∎

bmt-2012-power-6b.title: Induction
bmt-2012-power-6b.body:
By part (a), $x_n=3x_{n-1}-x_{n-2}$ for $n\ge2$, with $x_1=1=F_1$ and $x_2=2=F_3$.

The odd-indexed Fibonacci numbers satisfy the same recurrence: $F_{2n+1}=F_{2n}+F_{2n-1}=(F_{2n-1}+F_{2n-2})+F_{2n-1}=2F_{2n-1}+(F_{2n-1}-F_{2n-3})=3F_{2n-1}-F_{2n-3}$.

So $F_{2n-1}$ and $x_n$ satisfy the same recurrence with the same first two values ($n=1,2$), hence $x_n=F_{2n-1}$ for all $n\ge1$. (Also $x_0=1=F_{-1}$ if $F_{-1}=1$ is used.) ∎

bmt-2012-power-8.title: Strong induction with congruences
bmt-2012-power-8.body:
Write $a_n=s_n$. By Problem 7, $a_0,\dots,a_7$ are integers (and $a_n\ge1$). Let $n\ge8$ and suppose $a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}$ are positive integers; we show $a_n$ is an integer.

**Step 1: consecutive terms are coprime** (for indices $<n$). Suppose a prime $p$ divides $a_k$ and $a_{k-1}$ with $4\le k<n$. From $a_ka_{k-4}=a_{k-1}a_{k-3}+a_{k-2}^2$ we get $p\mid a_{k-2}^2$, so $p\mid a_{k-2}$. Then $p\mid a_{k-1},a_{k-2}$, and the same argument applied at index $k-1$ (if $k-1\ge4$) gives $p\mid a_{k-3}$, and so on down to $p\mid a_4,a_3$, and then $a_5a_1=a_4a_2+a_3^2$ gives $p\mid a_3^2=1$, a contradiction. So $\gcd(a_k,a_{k-1})=1$.

**Step 2: $\gcd(a_k,a_{k-2}a_{k-3})=1$ for $k\le n-2$ (with $k\ge4$).** If $p\mid a_k$ and $p\mid a_{k-3}$, then from $a_{k+1}a_{k-3}=a_ka_{k-2}+a_{k-1}^2$ we get $p\mid a_{k-1}$, contradicting Step 1. If $p\mid a_k$ and $p\mid a_{k-2}$, then from $a_ka_{k-4}=a_{k-1}a_{k-3}+a_{k-2}^2$ we get $p\mid a_{k-1}a_{k-3}$, which is again impossible by Step 1 and the previous sentence.

**Step 3.** We have to show $M:=a_{n-4}$ divides $N:=a_{n-3}a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}^2$. Work modulo $M$, using the recurrences at indices $n-1,n-2,n-3$ (valid since $a_0..a_{n-1}$ are integers):

- $a_{n-3}a_{n-7}=a_{n-4}a_{n-6}+a_{n-5}^2\equiv a_{n-5}^2$,
- $a_{n-1}a_{n-5}=a_{n-2}a_{n-4}+a_{n-3}^2\equiv a_{n-3}^2$,
- $a_{n-2}a_{n-6}=a_{n-3}a_{n-5}+a_{n-4}^2\equiv a_{n-3}a_{n-5}$.

Then
$$a_{n-7}a_{n-6}\,N\equiv a_{n-6}a_{n-5}^2a_{n-1}+a_{n-7}a_{n-6}a_{n-2}^2\equiv a_{n-6}a_{n-5}a_{n-3}^2+a_{n-7}a_{n-5}a_{n-3}a_{n-2},$$
and since $a_{n-5}a_{n-3}\equiv a_{n-6}a_{n-2}$ the first term is $\equiv a_{n-6}^2a_{n-2}a_{n-3}$. So
$$a_{n-7}a_{n-6}N\equiv a_{n-3}a_{n-2}\left(a_{n-6}^2+a_{n-7}a_{n-5}\right)=a_{n-3}a_{n-2}\,a_{n-8}a_{n-4}\equiv0\pmod M,$$
using the recurrence at index $n-4$. By Step 2 (with $k=n-4$), $\gcd(a_{n-4},a_{n-6}a_{n-7})=1$, so $M\mid N$ and $a_n=N/M$ is an integer. ∎

bmt-2012-power-9.title: Smallest bad index
bmt-2012-power-9.body:
Fix a prime $p$ dividing some denominator, and let $m$ be the smallest index with $p\mid d_m$; since $a_0,\dots,a_7$ are integers, $m\ge8$. Say a rational is *$p$-integral* if $p$ does not divide its denominator; $p$-integral numbers are closed under $+,\times$. So $a_0,\dots,a_{m-1}$ are $p$-integral and $a_m$ is not.

**(1) $p\mid a_{m-4}$.** From $a_ma_{m-4}=a_{m-1}a_{m-3}+a_{m-2}^2$ the right side is $p$-integral. If $p\nmid a_{m-4}$ (i.e. $a_{m-4}$ is a $p$-adic unit, as it is $p$-integral and non-divisible by $p$), then $a_m=(\text{$p$-integral})/a_{m-4}$ would be $p$-integral. So $p$ divides the numerator of $a_{m-4}$.

**(2) $p\mid a_{m-6}$ or $p\mid a_{m-7}$.** Using the recurrence at indices $m,m-1,\dots,m-4$ one verifies the identity
$$a_{m-7}a_{m-6}a_m=a_{m-8}a_{m-2}a_{m-3}-a_{m-6}a_{m-4}a_{m-3}+a_{m-6}a_{m-5}a_{m-2}+a_{m-6}^2a_{m-1}+a_{m-7}a_{m-4}a_{m-2}.$$
(It is obtained by expanding $a_{m-7}a_{m-6}a_{m-4}a_m=a_{m-7}a_{m-6}(a_{m-1}a_{m-3}+a_{m-2}^2)$ repeatedly with the recurrences at indices $m-1,\dots,m-4$, which produces $a_{m-4}$ times the right side, and dividing by $a_{m-4}$. It can be confirmed by expanding both sides, or numerically with exact fractions.) The right side is $p$-integral and $a_m$ is not, so $a_{m-7}a_{m-6}$ must be divisible by $p$.

**(3) Two consecutive terms are divisible by $p$.**

- If $p\mid a_{m-6}$: the recurrence at $m-4$, $a_{m-4}a_{m-8}=a_{m-5}a_{m-7}+a_{m-6}^2$, gives $p\mid a_{m-5}a_{m-7}$. So $p\mid a_{m-5}$ (with $a_{m-4}$: consecutive) or $p\mid a_{m-7}$ (with $a_{m-6}$: consecutive).
- If $p\mid a_{m-7}$ but $p\nmid a_{m-6}$: the recurrence at $m-3$, $a_{m-3}a_{m-7}=a_{m-4}a_{m-6}+a_{m-5}^2$, gives $p\mid a_{m-5}$, consecutive with $a_{m-4}$.

**(4) Propagate downward.** Suppose $p$ divides two consecutive terms $a_j,a_{j-1}$ with $j\ge4$ (all $p$-integral). The recurrence $a_ja_{j-4}=a_{j-1}a_{j-3}+a_{j-2}^2$ gives $p\mid a_{j-2}$. Now $a_{j-1},a_{j-2}$ are consecutive and divisible by $p$; repeating (while the index is $\ge4$) we get $p\mid a_k$ for all $2\le k\le j$. If $j\ge4$ this includes $a_2,a_3,a_4$, as required.

In (3), the pairs found are $(a_{m-4},a_{m-5})$ with $j=m-4\ge4$, which is fine, or $(a_{m-6},a_{m-7})$ with $j=m-6$, which is $\ge4$ unless $m=8,9$:

- $m=8$: then $p\mid a_4$, $p\mid a_2$, $p\mid a_1$. The recurrence at $5$: $a_5a_1=a_4a_2+a_3^2$ gives $p\mid a_3^2$, so $p\mid a_3$. Thus $p\mid a_2,a_3,a_4$.
- $m=9$: then $p\mid a_5$, $p\mid a_3$, $p\mid a_2$. The recurrence at $6$: $a_6a_2=a_5a_3+a_4^2$ gives $p\mid a_4^2$, so $p\mid a_4$.

So in every case $p\mid a_2,a_3,a_4$. Finally, the same prime divides $d_i$ for the given $i$ only if $i\ge m$, so the statement holds for every $i$ and every prime $p\mid d_i$. ∎

bmt-2012-power-10.title: A linear recurrence, then an invariant
bmt-2012-power-10.body:
Let $G_n$ be the $3\times2n$ grid (3 rows, $2n$ columns of vertices). $g_0=1$ (empty graph), $g_1=3$, $g_2=11$.

Let $a_n$ be the number of perfect matchings of $G_n$ with the top-left and middle-left vertices deleted. Look at the middle-left vertex of $G_n$: it is matched either up, down (by symmetry, each leaving a graph counted by $a_n$) or right. If it is matched right, the top-left and bottom-left vertices are forced to match right too (their only remaining neighbours), leaving $G_{n-1}$. So
$$g_n=2a_n+g_{n-1}.\qquad(1)$$
In the graph counted by $a_n$ the bottom-left vertex has a single neighbour (to its right), so that edge is forced; the top and middle vertices of the second column then are a column of two. The top one is matched either down to the middle one (leaving $G_{n-1}$) or to its right neighbour; then the middle one is forced right, the next bottom one is forced right, and what remains is the same type of graph with $2$ fewer columns. So
$$a_n=g_{n-1}+a_{n-1}.\qquad(2)$$
From (1): $g_n-g_{n-1}=2a_n$ and $g_{n-1}-g_{n-2}=2a_{n-1}$. Subtracting and using (2): $g_n-2g_{n-1}+g_{n-2}=2(a_n-a_{n-1})=2g_{n-1}$, so
$$g_n=4g_{n-1}-g_{n-2}\quad(n\ge2).$$
Let $I_n=g_{n-1}^2+g_{n-2}^2-4g_{n-1}g_{n-2}$. Then $I_2=9+1-12=-2$, and
$$I_{n+1}=g_n^2+g_{n-1}^2-4g_ng_{n-1}=g_{n-1}^2+g_n(g_n-4g_{n-1})=g_{n-1}^2-g_ng_{n-2}.$$
With $g_n=4g_{n-1}-g_{n-2}$ this is $g_{n-1}^2-4g_{n-1}g_{n-2}+g_{n-2}^2=I_n$, so $I_n=-2$ for all $n\ge2$. Finally
$$g_ng_{n-2}=(4g_{n-1}-g_{n-2})g_{n-2}=4g_{n-1}g_{n-2}-g_{n-2}^2=g_{n-1}^2-I_n=g_{n-1}^2+2.\ ∎$$
(Check: $g_0,\dots,g_4=1,3,11,41,153$.)

bmt-2012-power-11.title: Forced chain along the boundary
bmt-2012-power-11.body:
Place the diamond so that its middle row is horizontal. Let $T$ be the top side of the top square, $B$ the bottom side of the bottom square, $L$ the left side of the leftmost square and $R$ the right side of the rightmost square.

**Claim.** If $L$ is not in the perfect matching $M$, then $T\in M$ and $B\in M$.

Let $T_0,T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ be the squares along the upper-left boundary staircase, from the top square $T_0$ to the leftmost square $T_{n-1}$, and let $w_k$ be the top-left corner of $T_k$. Each $T_k$ is the only square of the diamond containing $w_k$, so $w_k$ has exactly two neighbours: the vertex to its right (the top-right corner of $T_k$) and the vertex below it. The vertex below $w_k$ is the top-right corner of $T_{k+1}$, i.e. the right neighbour of $w_{k+1}$.

The vertex $w_{n-1}$ has as neighbours its right neighbour and the lower-left corner of $T_{n-1}$ (the other endpoint of $L$). If $L\notin M$, then $w_{n-1}$ is matched to its right neighbour. Then $w_{n-2}$ has two neighbours, its right neighbour and the vertex below it, which is the right neighbour of $w_{n-1}$ and is already used; so $w_{n-2}$ is matched to its right neighbour. Continuing, every $w_k$ is matched to its right neighbour, and for $k=0$ this edge is $T$. So $T\in M$. The lower-left corner of $T_{n-1}$ has only two neighbours too, so the mirror-image argument along the lower-left staircase gives $B\in M$. This proves the claim.

The diamond is symmetric under rotation by $90^\circ$ and reflections, so the claim holds for each extreme edge: if $R\notin M$ then $T,B\in M$; if $T\notin M$ or $B\notin M$ then $L,R\in M$.

Now suppose $T,B$ are not both in $M$ and $L,R$ are not both in $M$. Then one of $T,B$ is missing, which forces $L,R\in M$, a contradiction. Hence $T,B\in M$ or $L,R\in M$. ∎

bmt-2012-power-12a.title: Kuo's graphical condensation
bmt-2012-power-12a.body:
**Answer.** $A_nA_{n-2}=A_{n-1}A_{n-1}+A_{n-1}A_{n-1}$, so $m=2$ and $i=j=k=l=1$, with initial conditions $A_0=1$ (empty diamond) and $A_1=2$ (a $4$-cycle).

**Proof of the recurrence.** We use Kuo's graphical condensation theorem: if $G$ is a planar bipartite graph with colour classes of equal size, and $a,b,c,d$ are vertices that lie in this cyclic order on one face, with $a,c$ of one colour and $b,d$ of the other, then
$$M(G)M(G-\{a,b,c,d\})=M(G-\{a,b\})M(G-\{c,d\})+M(G-\{a,d\})M(G-\{b,c\}),$$
where $M$ counts perfect matchings.

Take $G$ the Aztec diamond graph of size $n\ge2$ and, on the outer face, $a$ the left end of the topmost edge, $b$ the upper end of the rightmost edge, $c$ the right end of the bottommost edge, $d$ the lower end of the leftmost edge. They are in cyclic (clockwise) order and alternate in colour (checkerboard colouring of the grid). Rotation by $90^\circ$ maps $a\to b\to c\to d\to a$, so the four graphs $G-\{a,b\}$, $G-\{b,c\}$, $G-\{c,d\}$, $G-\{d,a\}$ are all isomorphic.

*Removing $a,b$.* Each outer corner vertex of the diamond on a boundary staircase has only two neighbours. After deleting $a$ and $b$, the vertices of the north-east staircase and of the south-east staircase each get a vertex of degree $1$ that propagates: matching a degree-one vertex forces its edge, and this forces the next vertex on the staircase, and so on. These forced edges ($2n-1$ of them) remove the whole north-east and south-east outer layers, and what remains is exactly the Aztec diamond graph of size $n-1$ (shifted by one unit). So $M(G-\{a,b\})=A_{n-1}$. (I checked the shape that remains for $n=3,4,5$ by computer.) Similarly, removing all four vertices leaves, after forced edges, the Aztec diamond of size $n-2$, so $M(G-\{a,b,c,d\})=A_{n-2}$.

Kuo's identity becomes $A_nA_{n-2}=A_{n-1}^2+A_{n-1}^2=2A_{n-1}^2$. With $A_0=1$, $A_1=2$ this gives $A_2=8$, $A_3=64$, $A_4=1024$ (confirmed by exhaustive computer counts). ∎
